To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the roles of teacher as supervisor of student teacher, teacher as co-instructor of a university course, and teacher as teacher educator are new roles for teachers in the professional development school movement.
teachers' new roles in professional development schools are complex and require a great deal of professional development.

(a) teacher educators' perceptions of their roles and their beliefs about their own professional development influence their enactment of those roles; (b) teacher educators' enactment of their roles is influenced by the institutional context of their work; and (c) the institutional context of teacher educators' work can influence the enactment of their roles in ways that are not always consistent with the intentions of the reform.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the roles of teacher as teacher educator, and the implications for the education of teachers.
the ways teachers are taking up new roles as they work with student teachers and as they co-instruct university classes.
the development of teacher leadership in professional development schools as part of the larger movement to restructure schooling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

teacher educators should be more aware of their role in the development of teachers and that they should be more aware that the role of teacher educators is a complex one that requires a variety of competencies.
the research literature does not yet provide an adequate basis for determining whether the professional development schools movement will succeed or fail.
the teacher as teacher educator in the professional development schools is not a new role but an extension of a teacher’s traditional role as a teacher.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
teachers are taking on new roles as teacher educators in professional development schools and that these roles are changing the contexts for learning and teaching.

we have found that teacher leaders, in general, and teachers as teacher educators in particular, are able to make significant contributions to the professional development of teachers and students, but only when they have the support and encouragement of administrators and university faculty and when the school and university are able to work together in a mutually supportive relationship.
we are interested in how teachers are taking up new roles and responsibilities in the restructuring of schools.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of the teacher as teacher educator is a critical component of a successful PDS partnership.
teachers are capable of assuming new roles and responsibilities if they are provided with appropriate support, resources, and recognition.
teachers are capable of taking on new roles in professional development schools.
